newsitem.title: USA: Saudis report progress on bomb investigation.
newsitem.headline: Saudis report progress on bomb investigation.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's defence minister said on Wednesday his government was making progress in the investigation of a truck bombing that killed 19 U.S. troops, but added that the probe would not be rushed.

"We have not finished the investigation. We are not pointing fingers yet at anybody," Defence Minister Prince Sultan told reporters during a visit to the Defence Department when asked about the June 25 bombing near Dhahran.

"We are trying to make sure justice is seen to be done and therefore we don't want to rush the investigation unnecessarily. But there is progress," Sultan told reporters as he was greeted by U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen for talks on Gulf defence cooperation.

Sultan, the brother of Saudi King Fahd, did not elaborate on the progress or say whether any links had been established to any other country, such as Iran, which has been accused by Washington of sponsoring anti-Western terrorism.

The Pentagon meeting came midway through a five-day Washington visit by senior Saudi ministers to reaffirm close ties marred by U.S. concerns over the probe into the truck bombing at the Khobar Towers military housing complex.

Washington has complained that Saudi Arabia is not sharing enough information with the FBI on its investigation of the Dhahran blast, which followed another Saudi car bombing in Riyadh in late 1995 that killed five Americans.
"Our cooperation with our friends is going in an excellent way and as soon as all the investigation is complete we plan to reveal all the details," Sultan said.

He met President Bill Clinton on Tuesday and will hold talks with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Thursday, The Saudi delegation, which includes the foreign, oil and trade ministers, will stay until Friday.
Both the prince and Cohen stressed to reporters the long and close ties between Washington.
A joint statement issued afterwards said they discussed improved security for U.S, military personnel in the kingdom.
The statement said Sultan invited the new U.S. defence secretary to visit Saudi Arabia and that Cohen hoped to travel to the Gulf later this year.

The White House and Defence Department have repeatedly stressed U.S. determination to protect the security of more than 6,000 American troops stationed in Saudi Arabia. Most of those troops were moved to a remote, heavily-guarded desert airbase last summer after the bombing.

In a reminder of the continued threat in Saudi Arabia, the U.S. embassy warned Americans in the kingdom on Tuesday to raise their guard against further attacks following fresh threats by a leading Islamic dissident.

The prince said earlier this month that the kingdom was interested in the possible multibillion-dollar purchase of perhaps 100 Lockheed Martin Corp. F-16 fighter jets to replace Saudi Arabia's ageing fleet of 114 F-5s. But he said he would not bring a firm order for such jets with him.

"At the moment, there is no request pending on this issue and there are discussions between the Royal Saudi Air Force and manufacturers of different weapons systems," Sultan at the Pentagon on Wednesday.
"This is not new. They have been doing this for awhile and probably will continue until they come to a final conclusion."
Israel has expressed concern about any F-16 sale to Saudi Arabia, which already flies sophisticated McDonnell Douglas Corp. F-15 fighter and attack jets.
